::: {.callout-tip title="Source & scope"}
All figures are from the **117th Meeting of the National Accounts Committee**, held on 14 May 2026 under the chairmanship of the Secretary, Ministry of Planning and Development. Q3 estimates are **provisional**; Q1 and Q2 estimates have been **revised** from those approved at the 116th NAC meeting. The 9-month average growth rate of 4.0% falls within the State Bank of Pakistan's projected range of **3.75 – 4.75 percent**.
:::

---

# Q3 FY 2025-26 — Provisional Estimates

## Sector-level headline growth

Overall GDP grew at **3.99 percent** in Q3 FY 2025-26 (reported as 4.0%). All three major sectors contributed positively.

| Sector | Q3 Growth | Status |
|:-------|:---------:|:-------|
| [**Agriculture**]{.sector-row} | [3.01%]{.pos} | All five sub-sectors positive |
| [**Industry**]{.sector-row} | [4.65%]{.pos} | LSM-driven; two sub-sectors in contraction |
| [**Services**]{.sector-row} | [4.18%]{.pos} | All eight sub-sectors positive |
| [**Overall GDP**]{.sector-row} | [3.99%]{.pos} | Within SBP 3.75–4.75% projected range |

---

## Agriculture — Q3 FY 2025-26 {#sec-agri-q3}

All five agricultural sub-sectors posted positive growth — a notable improvement on earlier quarters. Livestock remains the single largest sub-sector, contributing approximately 61% of agricultural GDP and around 11% of total GDP.

| Sub-sector | Q3 Growth | Note |
|:-----------|:---------:|:-----|
| Livestock | [+3.70%]{.pos} | Largest sub-sector; ~61% of agri GDP |
| Other crops | [+2.27%]{.pos} | Q1 revised sharply upward from −6.90% |
| Forestry | [+1.62%]{.pos} | — |
| Fishing | [+1.37%]{.pos} | Both Q1 & Q2 revised upward |
| Important crops | [+1.10%]{.pos} | Wheat 29 MT; rice ~9 MT (above estimates) |

::: {.callout-note title="Analytical note — wheat and rice"}
Wheat output reached **29 million tonnes** despite deeply negative farm economics — input costs (diesel, fertiliser) exceeded support prices, yet farmers had no viable alternative crop. Rice production hit approximately **9 million tonnes**, above earlier estimates despite flood-damaged acreage, due to a favourable late-season weather window. Cotton remained weak at around **4.8 million bales**, below the historical baseline, with downstream consequences for the textile sector.
:::

---

## Industry — Q3 FY 2025-26 {#sec-industry-q3}

Industry grew 4.65% in Q3, almost entirely on the back of large-scale manufacturing at 9.53%. Two sub-sectors contracted, with electricity recording a sharp double-digit decline.

| Sub-sector | Q3 Growth | Note |
|:-----------|:---------:|:-----|
| Large-scale manufacturing (LSM) | [+9.53%]{.pos} | Main drivers: apparel, automobiles, cement |
| Construction | [+0.48%]{.pos} | High base: +14.27% in Q3 FY25 |
| Mining & quarrying | [−2.55%]{.neg} | Continued contraction |
| Electricity, gas & water supply | [−13.53%]{.neg} | Base-year artefact — see note below |

::: {.callout-warning title="Methodological note — electricity contraction"}
The **−13.53%** contraction in electricity, gas and water supply is primarily a **base-year statistical artefact**. In Q3 FY 2024-25, this sub-sector recorded +129% growth because PKR 2,842 billion in circular debt payments were recognised in that period. The current-year figure reflects the reversal of that one-off effect. However, the underlying structural problem — circular debt stock of PKR 2,842B and high industrial tariffs — remains unresolved and continues to impair manufacturing competitiveness.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Quality of growth — class discussion point"}
LSM growth is concentrated in **three sub-sectors**: apparel assembly, automobile assembly, and cement. All three have limited domestic value-added content relative to their measured output:

- Automobile "production" in Pakistan is primarily final assembly of imported kits — value added is a small fraction of the unit price.
- Apparel assembly is the **lowest-margin** segment of the textile value chain.
- Assembly-type growth **does not absorb** the 3–4 million new labour force entrants per year at the scale required for the Lewis dual-sector transformation.
:::

---

## Services — Q3 FY 2025-26 {#sec-services-q3}

Services posted 4.18% growth with all eight sub-sectors contributing positively. Information & communication and public administration were the fastest-growing components.

| Sub-sector | Q3 Growth |
|:-----------|:---------:|
| Information & communication | [+9.78%]{.pos} |
| Public administration & social security | [+8.88%]{.amber-val} |
| Education | [+4.14%]{.pos} |
| Wholesale & retail trade | [+4.13%]{.pos} |
| Health & social work | [+4.07%]{.pos} |
| Other private services | [+3.35%]{.pos} |
| Finance & insurance | [+2.90%]{.pos} |
| Transportation & storage | [+2.02%]{.pos} |

::: {.callout-warning title="Methodological note — government services growth"}
Public administration & social security grew **8.88%** in real terms during a stated period of fiscal consolidation. This estimate is derived from **budgeted** rather than **actual** expenditure. A downward revision is expected in October 2026 once final spending outturns are incorporated. The same caveat applies to education (+4.14%) and health (+4.07%), both of which are largely remuneration-based estimates.
:::

# Q1 & Q2 Revisions — 116th vs 117th NAC

The 117th NAC meeting also approved revised estimates for Q1 and Q2 FY 2025-26. The overall pattern: **agriculture and services revised upward; industry revised downward**, with construction the dominant drag in both quarters.

## Overall GDP revisions

| Quarter | Old estimate | Revised estimate | Change |
|:--------|:-----------:|:----------------:|:------:|
| Q1 FY 2025-26 | 3.63% | [3.92%]{.pos} | [+0.29 pp ▲]{.rev-up} |
| Q2 FY 2025-26 | 3.89% | [4.05%]{.pos} | [+0.16 pp ▲]{.rev-up} |

---

## Agriculture revisions

| Sub-sector | Q1 old | Q1 revised | Q2 old | Q2 revised |
|:-----------|:------:|:----------:|:------:|:----------:|
| **Agriculture total** | 2.72% | [2.95% ▲]{.rev-up} | 1.76% | [2.64% ▲]{.rev-up} |
| Other crops | −6.90% | [+1.93% ▲]{.rev-up} | −5.69% | [+2.39% ▲]{.rev-up} |
| Fishing | 0.91% | [2.45% ▲]{.rev-up} | 0.77% | [1.47% ▲]{.rev-up} |
| Livestock | 6.18% | [4.67% ▼]{.rev-dn} | — | — |

The large Q1 upgrade in other crops (from −6.90% to +1.93%) and Q2 upgrade (from −5.69% to +2.39%) drove most of the overall agriculture revision. Livestock was revised downward in Q1 from 6.18% to 4.67%.

---

## Industry revisions

| Sub-sector | Q1 old | Q1 revised | Q2 old | Q2 revised |
|:-----------|:------:|:----------:|:------:|:----------:|
| **Industry total** | 8.86% | [7.80% ▼]{.rev-dn} | 7.40% | [6.68% ▼]{.rev-dn} |
| Electricity & water supply | 24.51% | [21.38% ▼]{.rev-dn} | — | — |
| Construction | 19.22% | [15.93% ▼]{.rev-dn} | 10.53% | [6.42% ▼]{.rev-dn} |

Construction is the primary driver of industry's downward revision in both quarters — cut from 19.22% to 15.93% in Q1 and from 10.53% to 6.42% in Q2.

---

## Services revisions

| Sub-sector | Q1 old | Q1 revised | Q2 old | Q2 revised |
|:-----------|:------:|:----------:|:------:|:----------:|
| **Services total** | 2.44% | [3.16% ▲]{.rev-up} | 3.69% | [3.83% ▲]{.rev-up} |
| Information & communication | −29.66% | [−7.63% ▲]{.rev-up} | −5.95% | [−1.27% ▲]{.rev-up} |
| Wholesale & retail trade | — | — | 4.46% | [4.66% ▲]{.rev-up} |

The dramatic revision in information & communication — from −29.66% to −7.63% in Q1 — drove most of the services upgrade. The sector appears to have suffered from initial data gaps that have since been partially filled.

---

# Key Observations for Class Discussion

::: {.callout-note title="1. Growth is real — but lopsided"}
The 4% headline figure is within the SBP forecast band and represents a genuine recovery from the 2022-23 crisis. However, it rests on three LSM sub-sectors (apparel assembly, automobiles, cement) with limited employment creation. The **Lewis dual-sector mechanism** requires broad industrial absorption of agricultural surplus labour — agriculture employs ~37% of the workforce but contributes only ~22% of GDP. This growth pattern does not resolve that structural imbalance.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="2. The revision pattern reveals a structural story"}
Across both Q1 and Q2, agriculture and services were revised upward; industry was revised downward — and **construction drove the downgrade in both quarters**. This pattern is consistent with an economy where formal capital investment in productive capacity remains subdued even as macro conditions stabilise.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="3. Electricity contraction is partly statistical — but the underlying problem is real"}
The −13.53% electricity figure reflects a base-year effect from prior-year circular debt clearance. The underlying crisis — circular debt stock of **PKR 2,842 billion** (2.7% of GDP), electricity tariffs raised ~PKR 5/kWh in FY25, and industrial tariffs among the highest in the region — remains unresolved and continues to erode manufacturing competitiveness.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="4. Data methodology requires scrutiny"}
Two methodological concerns warrant critical attention:

1. **Private investment in construction and SMEs** is estimated via survey pro-formas that are not cross-checked against SBP credit-to-private-sector data, utility connections, or construction material output indices — making the investment series difficult to validate independently.

2. **Government services growth** is based on budgeted rather than actual expenditure. The National Accounts Member post at PBS has been vacant for over two years — an institutional capacity gap that compromises the quality of national accounts across multiple dimensions.

Critical reading of official statistics is itself a core economics competency.
:::
